podcast.title: Comparison to other bands
podcast.body: Felix Contreras, an NPR contributor, compared Molo's sound, particularly its horn arrangements, to bands like Chicago and Blood, Sweat & Tears, while also likening the band to "Santana on steroids." "Contreras also likenes the horn arrangements within Molo to what was happening with the band Chicago. I can hear a little bit of blood, sweat, and tears in there too."

podcast.title: Discovery by Bill Graham
podcast.body: Molo, originally named The Malibu's, was discovered by Bill Graham, who also played a significant role in Santana's early career. "His band Molo was originally called the Malibu's, and they were also discovered by Bill Graham."

srcs.episode: Ep. 25 - The Hispanic Influence on 70s Popular Music

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonder Status
podcast.body: Molo is considered a one-hit wonder by Pop Chart standards due to the singular success of "Suavecito," despite producing four albums. "By Pop Chart standards, Molo is what we would call a one-hit wonder."

srcs.episode: Ep. 25 - The Hispanic Influence on 70s Popular Music

podcast.title: Post-Molo Career and Death
podcast.body: After making four albums with Molo and doing some work with his brother Carlos's band, Jorge Santana eventually stopped being a full-time musician. He completed one more album, "Restoration," before his death in May 2020 at the age of 68. "Molo made four albums in all, and Jorge did do some work with Carlos's band, but eventually he stopped being a full-time musician."

srcs.episode: Ep. 25 - The Hispanic Influence on 70s Popular Music

podcast.title: Record Label Pressure
podcast.body: The band experienced pressure from their record label to produce top 40 hits, which was difficult for Jorge Santana and Molo. This pressure may have contributed to their limited mainstream success beyond "Suavecito." "In fact, pressure from their record label to do just that was hard on Jorge and his band."
